title: January 6 United States Capitol attack
wiki_lead:
On January 6, 2021, the United States Capitol in Washington, D.C., was attacked by a mob of supporters of President Donald Trump. Academic debate exists about whether to characterize the event as an attempted coup, an attempted self-coup, or neither. The attack happened two months after Trump's defeat in the 2020 presidential election. Attackers sought to keep him in power by preventing a joint session of Congress from counting the Electoral College votes to formalize the victory of then president-elect Joe Biden. The attack was unsuccessful in preventing the certification of the election results. According to the bipartisan House select committee that investigated the incident, the attack was the culmination of a plan by Trump to overturn the election. Within 36 hours, five people died: one was shot by the Capitol Police, another died of a drug overdose, and three died of natural causes, including a police officer who died of a stroke a day after being assaulted by rioters and collapsing at the Capitol. Many people were injured, including 174 police officers. Four officers who responded to the attack died by suicide within seven months. Damage caused by attackers exceeded $2.7 million. 
Called to action by Trump on January 5 and 6, thousands of his supporters had gathered in Washington, D.C., to support his false claims that the 2020 election had been "stolen by emboldened radical-left Democrats", and to demand that then–vice president Mike Pence and Congress reject Biden's victory. Starting at noon on January 6, at a "Save America" rally on the Ellipse, Trump gave a speech in which he repeated false claims of election irregularities and said, "If you don't fight like hell, you're not going to have a country anymore". As Congress began the electoral vote count, thousands of attendees, some armed, walked to the Capitol, and hundreds breached police perimeters. Among the rioters were leaders of the Proud Boys and the Oath Keepers extremist militia groups.
The FBI estimates 2,000–2,500 people entered the Capitol during the attack. Some vandalized and looted, including in the offices of House speaker Nancy Pelosi and other Congress members. Rioters assaulted Capitol Police officers and journalists. Capitol Police evacuated and locked down both chambers of Congress and several buildings in the Complex. Rioters occupied the empty Senate chamber, while federal law enforcement officers defended the evacuated House floor. Pipe bombs were found at the Democratic National Committee and Republican National Committee headquarters, and Molotov cocktails were discovered in a vehicle near the Capitol. Trump resisted sending the National Guard to quell the mob. That afternoon, in a Twitter video, he restated false claims about the election and told his supporters to "go home in peace". The Capitol was cleared of rioters by mid-evening, and the electoral vote count was resumed and completed by the morning of January 7, concluding with Pence declaring the final electoral vote count in favor of President-elect Biden. Pressured by his cabinet, the threat of removal, and resignations, Trump conceded to an orderly transition of power in a televised statement.
A week after the attack, the House of Representatives impeached Trump for incitement of insurrection, making him the only U.S. president to be impeached twice. After Trump had left office, the Senate voted 57–43 in favor of conviction, but fell short of the required two-thirds, resulting in his acquittal. Senate Republicans blocked a bill to create a bipartisan independent commission to investigate the attack, so the House instead approved a select investigation committee. They held public hearings, voted to subpoena Trump, and recommended that the Department of Justice (DOJ) prosecute him. Following a special counsel investigation, Trump was indicted on four charges, all dismissed following his 2024 election to the presidency. Trump and elected Republican officials have promoted a revisionist history of the event by downplaying the severity of the violence, spreading conspiracy theories, and portraying those charged with crimes as hostages and martyrs.
Of the 1,424 people then charged with federal crimes relating to the event, 1,010 pled guilty, and 1,060 were sentenced, 64% of them to jail time. Some participants were linked to far-right extremist groups or conspiratorial movements, including the Oath Keepers, Proud Boys, and Three Percenters, some of whom were convicted of seditious conspiracy. Enrique Tarrio, then chairman of the Proud Boys, received the longest sentence, a 22-year prison term. No one was charged with the crime of insurrection.  In 2022, Biden signed a new law to clarify how electoral votes are to be counted.  On January 20, 2025, upon taking office again, Trump granted clemency to all January 6 rioters, including those convicted of violent offenses.

grok_lead: On January 6, 2021, thousands of supporters of outgoing President Donald Trump gathered to protest the certification of the 2020 presidential election results at the United States Capitol in Washington, D.C. Trump and many of his supporters claimed the election involved widespread voter fraud and irregularities. More than 60 lawsuits, Republican and Democratic state officials, and Trump's own Attorney General and Department of Justice concluded that the evidence presented was insufficient to change any state's certified outcome. At a rally near the White House, Trump repeated those claims, urged supporters to march to the Capitol, said they should "peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard," and said "we fight like hell, and if you don't fight like hell you're not going to have a country anymore." During and after the speech, parts of the crowd marched to the Capitol, where some removed or breached outer barriers, pushed past or overwhelmed police lines, broke windows and doors, and entered the building, disrupting the joint session of Congress for several hours. During the occupation Trump posted that Vice President Mike Pence "didn't have the courage to do what should have been done" to block certification and, at 4:17 p.m., released a video telling supporters to go home while repeating that the election had been stolen. Five deaths were associated with the events. The District of Columbia Office of the Chief Medical Examiner ruled the only homicide to be the officer-involved shooting of protester Ashli Babbitt as she attempted to climb through a broken window into the Speaker's Lobby; federal prosecutors declined charges and a U.S. Capitol Police internal investigation found the conduct lawful and within policy. The remaining four deaths were ruled natural or accidental: Rosanne Boyland (accidental acute amphetamine intoxication), Kevin Greeson and Benjamin Philips (hypertensive atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease), and Officer Brian Sicknick, who died of strokes the following day. The examiner found no evidence of trauma or allergic reaction to chemical spray but stated that "all that transpired played a role in his condition." Early reports that Sicknick had been beaten to death with a fire extinguisher were later contradicted by the official ruling. Four additional officers who responded later died by suicide in the days to months afterward. More than 140 police officers were injured, according to the Justice Department, including U.S. Capitol Police and Metropolitan Police officers. A 2022 GAO report found that about 114 Capitol Police officers alone reported injuries. Direct property damage was estimated at about $2.73 million; broader related costs reached approximately $2.7 billion. The House January 6 Select Committee, composed of seven Democrats and two Republicans who had voted to impeach Trump, concluded that Trump had engaged in a multi-part effort to overturn the election; Trump and Republican critics disputed the committee's composition, process, and conclusions. The committee was formed after Congress failed to create an independent, bipartisan commission modeled on the 9/11 Commission. H.R. 3233, negotiated by Representatives Bennie Thompson (D-MS) and John Katko (R-NY), would have established a ten-member commission split evenly between the two parties, with subpoena power; it passed the House 252â175 on May 19, 2021, with Democratic support and 35 Republicans, but on May 28 fell short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a Senate filibuster, 54â35, with all Democrats present and six Republicans voting to proceed. The House impeached Trump for incitement of insurrection; the Senate acquitted him 57â43. Federal prosecutors charged 1,583 individuals. The large majority faced lower-level offenses such as misdemeanor trespass, parading, or disorderly conduct; a substantial minority faced felony assault or related counts. Seditious conspiracy charges were brought against 18 defendants affiliated with the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys, of whom 14 were convicted. By January 2025, 1,270 had been convicted, mostly by plea. A January 20, 2025, presidential proclamation granted full pardons to nearly all of those convicted, including those charged with assaulting officers, and commuted the sentences of 14 others, while directing dismissal of remaining pending cases. The proclamation described the action as ending "a grave national injustice" and beginning "a process of national reconciliation." The action drew objections from some officers, victims' families, and members of both parties. In 2026 the Justice Department moved to vacate remaining seditious conspiracy convictions; courts granted the requests, with some judges expressing disagreement while acknowledging executive authority over charging decisions. Its characterization as an insurrection, a riot, or a breach remains disputed. Those applying the stronger terms cite the forcible interruption of electoral certification, assaults on officers, and seditious-conspiracy convictions of certain organized groups; those rejecting those terms note that no defendant was charged under the federal insurrection statute, most prosecutions were for trespass or parading, and the Senate acquitted Trump of incitement. Debates continue over the relative roles of organized groups versus spontaneous crowd action, the degree of premeditation, documented intelligence and security shortfalls, and Trump's rally rhetoric.
